# International rental property for a US investor

Nine countries assessed for a US-resident investor buying residential property to
rent out: **Costa Rica, Hungary, France, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Greece, Mexico,
Panama**.

**Last revised:** 2026-08-17

## What this document does and does not answer

It answers the **legal and regulatory** question well: who may buy, under what
instrument, what tax applies to a non-resident landlord, what happens on death,
and whether a short-let strategy survives the regulator.

It does **not** answer the financial question. There is no gross rental yield,
price-to-rent ratio or days-on-market figure for any of the nine countries in
this study, and none for the United States. **Whether any of these markets beats
a US-domestic rental is not established here, in either direction.** Six of the
nine have no usable price or rent level at all, and no price-per-square-foot
conversion is published because no source establishes the measured-area basis
that would make such a conversion like-for-like.

Use it to eliminate candidates and avoid specific traps. Do not use it to pick a
winner on returns.

| Hungary | ✗ *(income treaty also terminated)* | 15% *(general rule)* | **discretionary permit** |
| Mexico | ✗ | **25% on gross**, no deductions; net-basis election open to US residents | **trust only** in coastal/border zone |

"—" means this run established nothing. It is not a zero. Sources and the full
picture are in [the deliverable](international-rental-property.md).

## Five things worth knowing before anything else

1. **Six of the nine have no US estate tax treaty**, so a US decedent's property
   there can be taxed twice, with only the narrow IRC § 2014 credit as a fallback.
   This eliminates more candidates than any other single test and costs nothing to
   check.
2. **Spain and Mexico tax a US landlord on gross rent with no deductions.** The
   effective burden is worse than the headline rate suggests: on an assumed 30%
   cost ratio, a US owner in Spain bears about 1.8× what an EU owner does, not the
   1.26× the 24%-versus-19% headline implies. The 30% is an illustrative
   assumption, not a sourced figure — the actual multiple moves with the cost
   ratio.
3. **Three countries gate or block acquisition.** Costa Rica bars non-residents
   from the 200-metre coastal strip and all islands by statute; Mexico permits only
   a 50-year bank trust in the restricted zone, conferring no rights in rem;
   Hungary requires a refusable per-property permit. Italy's reciprocity gate is
   real; a 1949 treaty grants US citizens national treatment on immovable
   property, but whether Italy's foreign ministry treats that as satisfying the
   gate could not be confirmed.
4. **Short-let rules are moving fast and against the non-resident.** Barcelona
   extinguishes every tourist-flat licence by November 2028; central Athens is
   frozen to new registrations **and a sale deletes an existing one**; Spain's
   national registry was annulled by the Supreme Court in mid-2026; Italy cut the
   volume ceiling from four apartments to two.
5. **Portugal's CIMT sets a flat 7.5% purchase tax on non-residents** with all
   reliefs disapplied — escapable only by becoming resident or by letting at a
   capped rent for at least 36 months in five years. The rate and its amending
   diploma are sourced to primary text; **its commencement date is not stated in
   that text and is not asserted here**, though a regulator's notice places the
   decree in force by late June 2026 [72].

## Decision order

1. **Can you buy, and what do you own?** Tenure first — trust, concession or
   title.
2. **What happens on death?** Estate treaty or not.
3. **What is the tax base**, not the rate? Ask about deductibility before
   comparing percentages.
4. **Does your rental strategy survive the regulator?** Especially for short-let.
5. **How long to recover possession?** Only France has a real figure: 8 months
   minimum, about two years in practice.
6. **Then the numbers** — which you will have to source elsewhere.

## How this was researched, and why the gaps look like this

102 search queries and 204 page fetches, of which 157 returned usable text and 47
failed (23%). Search ran through a single live engine for the whole run, so no query could form
the two independent samples the method requires — 94 returned one sample and 8
returned none at all.

The gaps are not random. Retrieval ran through a host-side fetch service, and
several classes of source refuse it or defeat it: **Greece's tax authority, the
IMF, Spain's housing ministry and the Council of Europe returned HTTP 403; every
US State Department Investment Climate Statement returned an error body; Mexico
City's servers timed out; Panama's gazette failed on DNS, PDF parsing and a
scanned image with no text layer.** That is why the risk dimension is thin and why
Greece, Mexico and Panama are the least covered — a property of this run's
retrieval path, not of those countries.
